passages.happening:
Joseph has been taken down to Egypt. “An Egyptian named Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh and captain of the guard, bought him from the Ishmaelites who had taken him there” (verse 1).

“And the LORD was with Joseph, and he became a successful man, serving in the household of his Egyptian master” (verse 2).

Potiphar sees that the LORD is with him (verse 3). He makes Joseph his personal servant and puts him in charge of everything he owns (verse 4). “The LORD blessed the Egyptian's household on account of him” (verse 5).

Potiphar leaves everything in Joseph's care and thinks of nothing “except the food he ate” (verse 6). “Now Joseph was well-built and handsome” (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
The story comes back to Joseph after the chapter on Judah. The contrast is deliberate. Judah, a free man among his own people, went to a woman he took for a prostitute. Joseph, a slave far from home, will refuse his master's wife at great cost.

Potiphar is ‘an officer of Pharaoh’. Pharaoh is the title of Egypt's king. ‘Captain of the guard’ is literally ‘chief of the slaughterers’. He was probably head of the king's bodyguard, or of those who carried out the king's sentences.

Now the refrain. ‘The LORD was with Joseph.’ It comes four times in this chapter (verses 2, 3, 21, 23). LORD in capital letters stands for God's own name, which is rare in Joseph's story. It gathers here, at the start and end of the chapter.

But look where Joseph is when the LORD is with him. He is a slave. He has been sold by his brothers and bought by a stranger. He does not go home. He is not set free. ‘The LORD was with him’ is not a promise that life will go well. It is a promise of presence, in slavery and, soon, in prison.

And look at the blessing. God promised Abraham that other peoples would be blessed through his family (12:3). Here an Egyptian household is blessed because of a Hebrew slave.

The last line, ‘well-built and handsome’, is a warning. It is the hinge to what comes next.
passages.later:
Stephen tells this part of the story: “they sold him as a slave into Egypt. But God was with him and rescued him from all his troubles” (Acts 7:9-10).

God's promise through Isaiah has the same shape: “When you pass through the waters, I will be with you” (Isaiah 43:2). Not around the waters. Through them. A psalm says, “Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for You are with me” (Psalm 23:4).
passages.asks: God was with Joseph while he was still a slave. Ask whether you think God's presence should always mean things go well. Then ask where he might be with you in a place you never chose to be.

passages.t: ‘How could I do such a great evil?’
passages.happening:
“After some time his master's wife cast her eyes upon Joseph and said, ‘Sleep with me’” (verse 7).

Joseph refuses. His master has trusted him with everything. “He has withheld nothing from me except you, because you are his wife. So how could I do such a great evil and sin against God?” (verse 9).

“Although Potiphar's wife spoke to Joseph day after day, he refused to go to bed with her or even be near her” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
Potiphar's wife is never named. She is the wife of a powerful man. Joseph is a slave in her house. This is not a romance between equals. She has power over him, and he has none over her.

She does not ask once. She keeps on, day after day. Joseph cannot leave the house. He cannot report her. In that world a slave's word counted for little against his mistress's. Saying no to her was dangerous.

Joseph gives two reasons. The first is loyalty: his master has trusted him with everything except her. To betray that trust would be a great evil. The second goes deeper: it would be a ‘sin against God’. Joseph is in a foreign land, far from his father, with no one from his family watching. He still lives before God.

And he keeps his distance. He refuses even ‘to be near her’. He does not trust himself to stand close to the fire and not be burned.
passages.later:
David, after his own sin, confessed in the same way: “Against You, You only, have I sinned and done what is evil in Your sight” (Psalm 51:4).

Paul gives Joseph's advice in one word: “Flee from sexual immorality” (1 Corinthians 6:18). And Hebrews says that Jesus “was tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin” (Hebrews 4:15).
passages.asks: Joseph said no again and again to someone who had power over him. Ask what you would do if no one you knew were watching. Then ask what it would mean to live as though God is always the one you answer to.

passages.happening:
One day Joseph goes into the house to work, and no servants are there (verse 11). “She grabbed Joseph by his cloak and said, ‘Sleep with me!’ But leaving his cloak in her hand, he escaped and ran outside” (verse 12).

She calls the servants. “Look,” she says, “this Hebrew has been brought to us to make sport of us. He came to me so he could sleep with me, but I screamed as loud as I could” (verse 14). She keeps his cloak beside her until her husband comes home (verse 16).

She tells him the same story: “The Hebrew slave you brought us came to me to make sport of me” (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
The house is empty. She grabs him. He runs, and leaves his cloak in her hand. He would rather lose his clothes than his integrity.

Then she lies. She turns the truth upside down. She is the one who grabbed him; she says he came at her. She is the one with power; she makes herself the victim.

Listen to how she speaks. To the servants she calls him ‘this Hebrew’, an outsider, a foreigner. She turns them against him because he is a foreigner. And she blames her husband: he ‘has been brought to us’. To her husband she says ‘the Hebrew slave you brought us’. The blame shifts a little each time she tells it.

For the second time in Joseph's story a piece of his clothing is used as false evidence. His brothers used his robe to deceive their father (37:31-33). Now his master's wife uses his cloak to deceive her husband.
passages.later:
Israel's law forbids exactly what she did: “You shall not spread a false report. Do not join the wicked by being a malicious witness” (Exodus 23:1).

Peter writes to people who suffer unjustly: “if you suffer for doing good and you endure it, this is commendable before God” (1 Peter 2:20).
passages.hard:
This story must be read with care. Here a powerful person preys on an enslaved one who cannot consent or refuse safely, and then lies. She is the one with power; he is the one with none.

This story is not a reason to disbelieve a person who reports sexual assault. It is about a woman with power falsely accusing a slave with none, to cover what she herself had done. It does not teach that people who report abuse are lying. Studies of reported sexual assaults have found that false reports are uncommon; one well-known study by David Lisak and colleagues (2010) judged about 6 in 100 reports at one university over ten years to be false. And many people who have been assaulted stay silent because they fear they will not be believed. Using this chapter to doubt them would turn the story on its head. The Bible's own law tells judges to look into a charge with care (Deuteronomy 19:18), not to dismiss it.

An Egyptian story, the Tale of Two Brothers, survives on a papyrus written in about 1215 BC, now in the British Museum. In it a married woman tries to seduce her husband's younger brother, is refused, and then claims he attacked her. The likeness shows that such a situation was known in that world. It is a comparison only; it does not show that either story borrowed from the other.

A word for anyone who is being pressured for sex, or for anything else, by someone with power over them: a boss, a teacher, a coach, a leader, an owner, a family member. You are not to blame for their pressure. Saying no is right, and it is not your fault if they punish you for it. Please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Joseph ran and lost his cloak, and then lost his good name. Ask whether you would choose to do right if you knew it would cost you. Then ask how you listen when someone without power tells you what was done to them.

passages.t: In prison, and the LORD with him
passages.happening:
Potiphar hears his wife's story “and he burned with anger” (verse 19). He has Joseph “thrown into the prison where the king's prisoners were confined” (verse 20).

“While Joseph was there in the prison, the LORD was with him and extended kindness to him, granting him favor in the eyes of the prison warden” (verses 20-21).

The warden puts all the prisoners under Joseph's care (verse 22). “The warden did not concern himself with anything under Joseph's care, because the LORD was with Joseph and gave him success in whatever he did” (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
Joseph did right, and he was punished for it. The chapter does not hide that. He is falsely accused, and no one hears his side.

Some readers wonder why Potiphar put him in prison rather than having him killed. The text does not say. Perhaps Potiphar doubted his wife; perhaps the prison simply came under his office. These are guesses.

The king's prison held the king's prisoners, people who had offended the court. That detail matters. It is where Joseph will meet two of Pharaoh's servants in the next chapter.

Then the refrain comes back. ‘The LORD was with him.’ In the pit, in Potiphar's house, and now in prison. The word ‘kindness’ here is the Hebrew chesed, God's loyal, faithful love. Every human loyalty has failed Joseph: his brothers sold him, his master's wife lied about him, his master believed her. God's loyalty has not.

And look at the pattern. In Potiphar's house his master ‘did not concern himself with anything’ (verse 6). In prison the warden ‘did not concern himself with anything’ (verse 23). Joseph has fallen lower, but God is doing the same thing again.

This does not make the injustice good. The text never says Potiphar's wife was right. It says God was not defeated by what she did.
passages.later:
A psalm looks back on these years: “They bruised his feet with shackles and placed his neck in irons, until his prediction came true and the word of the LORD proved him right” (Psalm 105:18-19).

Peter writes that Jesus, when he suffered unjustly, “entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23). And God promises, “Never will I leave you, never will I forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5).
passages.asks: Joseph was punished for doing right, and God was still with him. Ask whether you have read a hard season as proof that God had left you. Then ask what faithfulness looks like in the place where you are stuck today.
